title: Max and Mins
subtitle: Finding the highest and lowest points

slides.title: Highs and lows
slides.text:
The **absolute maximum** of a function is its highest point. The **absolute minimum** is its lowest point.

You will also hear them called the **global maximum** and **global minimum**. Same thing, different name.

Here is the graph of $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ on the interval $[-2, 2]$.
What is the height of the lowest point on this graph?
slides.hint: Find the lowest point on the curve, then read how high it is on the $y$-axis.
slides.explain: The lowest point is $(0, 1)$, so the absolute minimum is 1.

slides.text: What is the height of the highest point on this graph?
slides.hint: The graph is highest at the ends. Read the height of an end point.
slides.explain: The graph is highest at both ends, $(-2, 5)$ and $(2, 5)$. The absolute maximum is 5.

slides.title: Is there always a highest and lowest point?
slides.text:
No. Some functions have both, some have only one, and some have neither.

For each of the next graphs, decide: **is there a highest point? Is there a lowest point?** An arrow means the graph keeps going in that direction forever. An open circle means that point is not on the graph.
$f(x) = x^3$ on all real numbers. Which is true?
options: Both an absolute max and an absolute min
An absolute max, but no absolute min
An absolute min, but no absolute max
Neither one
slides.hint: Follow the arrows. Does the graph stop climbing on the right? Does it stop falling on the left?
slides.explain: The graph keeps climbing to the right and keeps falling to the left. There is no highest point and no lowest point.

slides.text: $f(x) = 1/(x^2 + 1)$ on all real numbers. Which is true?
options: Both an absolute max and an absolute min
An absolute max, but no absolute min
An absolute min, but no absolute max
Neither one
slides.hint: Find the top of the hill. Then ask: does the graph ever reach a lowest height out on the sides?
slides.explain: The highest point is $(0, 1)$. Out on the sides the graph gets closer and closer to 0 but never gets there, so there is no lowest point.

slides.text: This function is in two pieces and lives on $[0, 4]$. Which is true?
options: Both an absolute max and an absolute min
An absolute max, but no absolute min
An absolute min, but no absolute max
Neither one
slides.hint: Look at the open circle. Is there a lowest point on the left piece? What about the filled point just above it?
slides.explain: The highest point is $(0, 2)$. Near $x = 2$ the left piece heads down toward $-2$, but that point is open, so the graph never reaches it. The filled point at height $-1$ is higher, so something lower is always still available. There is no lowest point.

slides.text: $f(x) = (x - 2)^2$ on the interval $[1, 4]$. Which is true?
options: Both an absolute max and an absolute min
An absolute max, but no absolute min
An absolute min, but no absolute max
Neither one
slides.hint: Both ends are filled in. Find the lowest point and the highest point.
slides.explain: The lowest point is $(2, 0)$ and the highest point is $(4, 4)$. Both exist.

slides.text: $f(x) = x / (2 - x)$ on the interval $[0, 2)$. The dashed line is at $x = 2$. Which is true?
options: Both an absolute max and an absolute min
An absolute max, but no absolute min
An absolute min, but no absolute max
Neither one
slides.hint: What happens to the graph as it gets close to the dashed line? Where does it start?
slides.explain: The graph shoots upward near the dashed line, so there is no highest point. The lowest point is $(0, 0)$ where it starts.

slides.title: The max is a height
slides.text:
**The absolute maximum is a $y$-value**, a height. It is not the $x$-value.

For $f(x) = (x - 2)^2$ on $[1, 4]$ the absolute maximum is **4**. We say it **occurs at** $x = 4$.

So be careful. If someone asks for the maximum, they want a height. If they ask where it occurs, they want an $x$-value.
What is the absolute maximum of this function?
slides.hint: The maximum is a height. Read it off the $y$-axis.
slides.explain: The highest point is $(4, 4)$. The absolute maximum is 4.

slides.text: At what $x$-value does the absolute minimum occur?
slides.hint: The lowest point is where the curve touches the bottom. Which $x$ is under it?
slides.explain: The lowest point is $(2, 0)$. The minimum occurs at $x = 2$.

slides.text: What is the absolute minimum of this function?
slides.hint: The minimum is a height, not a location.
slides.explain: The lowest point is $(2, 0)$. The absolute minimum is 0.

slides.title: Your turn
slides.text: Here is a new graph. Find the highest and lowest points, if they exist. If a point does not exist, tap **None**.
What is the absolute maximum?
slides.hint: Find the top of the hill and read its height.
slides.explain: The top of the hill is $(1, 3)$. The absolute maximum is 3.

slides.text: What is the absolute minimum?
slides.hint: Compare the two ends of the graph. Which end is lower?
slides.explain: The left end $(-1, -1)$ is lower than the right end $(2.5, 0.75)$. The absolute minimum is $-1$.

slides.text: This is $f(x) = x^2$ on the **open** interval $(0, 3)$. Both ends are open circles. What is the absolute maximum?
slides.hint: Is the highest point on the graph an open circle? Can you ever stand on an open circle?
slides.explain: The graph heads up toward the open circle at height 9, but never reaches it. There is always a higher point closer to $x = 3$. There is no absolute maximum.

slides.title: The Extreme Value Theorem
slides.text:
**Extreme Value Theorem (EVT)**

If $f$ is **continuous** on a **closed interval** $[a, b]$, then $f$ has an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on $[a, b]$.

You need **both** conditions:
• continuous: no jumps, holes, or breaks
• closed interval: both endpoints are included

You will use this idea in questions all through this chapter.
Which two things must be true for the Extreme Value Theorem to apply?
options: $f$ is continuous and the interval is closed
$f$ is differentiable and the interval is open
$f'(x) = 0$ somewhere and $f$ is increasing
$f$ is continuous and the interval is open
slides.hint: The theorem has a word for the function and a word for the interval.
slides.explain: $f$ must be continuous, and the interval must be closed.

slides.text: Does the EVT guarantee a max and min for $f(x) = (x - 2)^2$ on $[1, 4]$?
options: Yes: continuous on a closed interval
No: the interval is open
No: $f$ is not continuous
slides.hint: Check each condition: continuous? closed?
slides.explain: A parabola is continuous everywhere, and $[1, 4]$ includes both endpoints. The theorem applies, and sure enough the graph has a highest and lowest point.

slides.text: Does the EVT guarantee a max and min for $f(x) = x^2$ on the **open** interval $(0, 3)$?
options: Yes: continuous on a closed interval
No: the interval is open
No: $f$ is not continuous
slides.hint: Look at the ends of the interval. Are they included?
slides.explain: The interval $(0, 3)$ leaves out the endpoints, so it is not closed. The theorem does not apply, and indeed the graph has no highest or lowest point.

slides.text: Does the EVT guarantee a max and min for this function on $[0, 4]$?
options: Yes: continuous on a closed interval
No: the interval is open
No: $f$ is not continuous
slides.hint: Look for a break in the graph.
slides.explain: The graph jumps at $x = 2$, so it is not continuous. The theorem does not apply. (This one has a max but no min.)

slides.text: Does the EVT guarantee a max and min for $f(x) = 1/x$ on $[-1, 1]$?
options: Yes: continuous on a closed interval
No: the interval is open
No: $f$ is not continuous
slides.hint: What is $f(0)$?
slides.explain: $1/x$ is undefined at $x = 0$, which is inside the interval. So $f$ is not continuous on $[-1, 1]$ and the theorem does not apply.

slides.title: A guarantee, not a test
slides.text:
When the conditions are met, the EVT **promises** that a max and min exist.

When the conditions are **not** met, the theorem promises nothing. The function might still have a max or min, or it might not. You have to look.
If a function is not continuous on $[a, b]$, it cannot have an absolute maximum there.
slides.hint: Does the theorem say what happens when its conditions fail?
slides.explain: The theorem only promises extremes when its conditions hold. When they fail, a function can still have a highest point. The piecewise graph earlier had a highest point, $(0, 2)$, even though it jumps.

slides.title: Local extreme values
slides.text:
A **local maximum** is a point that is higher than every other point **near it**, like the top of a hill.

A **local minimum** is a point that is lower than every other point near it, like the bottom of a valley.

This graph has a hilltop and a valley.
Which $x$-value is a **local maximum** of this graph?
slides.hint: Look for the top of the hill.
slides.explain: The hilltop is at $x = -1$. The valley is at $x = 1$.

slides.text: Is the local maximum at $x = -1$ also the absolute maximum?
options: Yes, it is the highest point on the graph
No, the graph keeps climbing to the right
slides.hint: Follow the arrow on the right side.
slides.explain: The graph climbs forever to the right, so there is no absolute maximum. The hilltop is only a local maximum.

slides.text: Every absolute maximum is also a local maximum.
slides.hint: The highest point of all is higher than everything. Is it higher than the points near it?
slides.explain: The highest point overall is certainly higher than the points near it.

slides.text: Every local maximum is also an absolute maximum.
slides.hint: Think of the hill on the graph you just saw.
slides.explain: A local maximum only has to beat the points near it. The hilltop on the last graph is a local maximum but not an absolute maximum.

slides.title: Critical points
slides.text:
A **critical point** is an $x$-value $c$ in the domain of $f$ where either

• $f'(c) = 0$ (the tangent line is flat), or
• $f'(c)$ **does not exist** (a sharp corner, a cusp, or a vertical tangent).

Look at five graphs. In each one, something is happening at $x = 0$. Decide what.
What is happening at $x = 0$?
options: A critical point, and a local maximum
A critical point, and a local minimum
A critical point, but **not** a local max or min
Not a critical point
slides.hint: Draw the tangent line at the top of the hill. Is it flat?
slides.explain: The tangent line is flat there, so $f'(0) = 0$. It is a critical point, and it is the top of a hill.

slides.text: What is happening at $x = 0$?
options: A critical point, and a local maximum
A critical point, and a local minimum
A critical point, but **not** a local max or min
Not a critical point
slides.hint: This hilltop is a sharp point. Can you draw a single tangent line there?
slides.explain: At a sharp point there is no single tangent line, so $f'(0)$ does not exist. That makes it a critical point, and it is the top of a hill.

slides.text: What is happening at $x = 0$?
options: A critical point, and a local maximum
A critical point, and a local minimum
A critical point, but **not** a local max or min
Not a critical point
slides.hint: Another sharp point. Is it a hill or a valley?
slides.explain: A corner means $f'(0)$ does not exist, so it is a critical point. It is the bottom of a valley.

slides.text: What is happening at $x = 0$?
options: A critical point, and a local maximum
A critical point, and a local minimum
A critical point, but **not** a local max or min
Not a critical point
slides.hint: The tangent line is flat. Does the graph turn around?
slides.explain: The tangent line is flat, so $f'(0) = 0$ and it is a critical point. But the graph keeps climbing straight through, so it is not a max or min.

slides.text: What is happening at $x = 0$?
options: A critical point, and a local maximum
A critical point, and a local minimum
A critical point, but **not** a local max or min
Not a critical point
slides.hint: The tangent line is straight up and down. Does the graph turn around?
slides.explain: A vertical tangent means $f'(0)$ does not exist, so it is a critical point. But the graph keeps climbing, so it is not a max or min.

slides.title: Critical points are only suspects
slides.text:
Notice what you just saw: a critical point **might** be a local max or min, and it might not.

But every local max and min has to be at a critical point. That is the next theorem.

slides.title: Fermat's Theorem
slides.text:
**Fermat's Theorem**

If $f$ has a local maximum or minimum at $c$, **and** $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then $f'(c) = 0$.

In words: at a smooth hilltop or valley, the tangent line is flat.

So local maxes and mins can only hide at critical points. **Critical points are the places to look.**

slides.title: Say it in your own words
slides.text: If $f$ has a local ___ at $c$ and $f$ is ___ at $c$, then $f'(c)$ = ___.
slides.hint: Think about what Fermat's Theorem needs about the function, and what it concludes about the slope.
slides.explain: If $f$ has a local extremum at $c$ and is differentiable there, then $f'(c) = 0$.

slides.title: It does NOT work in reverse
slides.text:
Fermat's Theorem goes one way:

local max or min and differentiable  $\Rightarrow$  $f'(c) = 0$.

It does **not** say the other direction. Look at $f(x) = x^3$. Here $f'(0) = 0$, but $x = 0$ is **not** a max or min.

**$f'(c) = 0$ does NOT mean there is a max or min at $c$.**
If $f'(c) = 0$, then $f$ must have a local maximum or local minimum at $c$.
slides.hint: Remember $f(x) = x^3$ at $x = 0$.
slides.explain: $f(x) = x^3$ has $f'(0) = 0$ but keeps climbing straight through. A flat tangent does not guarantee a max or min.

slides.text: $f(x) = (x^2 - 1)^3$ has $f'(x) = 6x(x^2 - 1)^2$, which is 0 at $x = -1, 0, 1$. Which of these are local extrema?
options: All three
Only $x = 0$
Only $x = -1$ and $x = 1$
None of them
slides.hint: Look at the graph near each of the three $x$-values. Does it turn around?
slides.explain: At $x = 0$ the graph bottoms out. At $x = \pm 1$ the tangent is flat but the graph passes straight through, so those are critical points that are not extrema.

slides.title: Finding critical points
slides.text:
To find the critical points of $f$:

1. Find $f'(x)$.
2. Solve $f'(x) = 0$.
3. Find where $f'(x)$ **does not exist** but $f(x)$ does.

Every $x$ you find is a critical point. Enter the $x$-values with the keypad, tap **Add to list** after each one, then check. Tap a number in your list to remove it.

Find the critical points of $f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 + 1$.

Its derivative is $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x = 3x(x - 2)$.
slides.hint: Set $3x(x - 2) = 0$ and set each factor equal to 0.
slides.explain: $3x(x - 2) = 0$ at $x = 0$ and $x = 2$. The derivative exists everywhere, so those are all of them.

slides.text:
Find the critical points of $f(x) = |x - 2|$.

Its derivative is $-1$ when $x < 2$ and $1$ when $x > 2$.
slides.hint: The derivative is never 0. Where does the graph have a sharp corner?
slides.explain: The derivative is never 0, but at the corner $x = 2$ the derivative does not exist. Since $f(2)$ exists, $x = 2$ is a critical point.

slides.text:
Find the critical points of $f(x) = x^(3/5)(4 - x)$.

Its derivative is $f'(x) = (12 - 8x) / (5x^(2/5))$.
slides.hint: Where is the top equal to 0? Where is the bottom equal to 0 (so $f'$ does not exist)?
slides.explain: The top is 0 when $12 - 8x = 0$, so $x = 1.5$. The bottom is 0 at $x = 0$, so $f'(0)$ does not exist, but $f(0)$ does. Both are critical points.

slides.text:
Try it: find the critical points of $f(x) = x^3 + 6x^2 - 15x$.

Its derivative is $f'(x) = 3x^2 + 12x - 15$.
slides.hint: Factor out the 3 first: $3(x^2 + 4x - 5)$. Then factor again.

slides.title: Finding the absolute max and min
slides.text:
Now we put it all together. Suppose $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$. The EVT says an absolute max and min exist. Where are they?

The highest and lowest points are either at an **endpoint**, or at a local max or min inside. And local extremes can only be at critical points. So:

**1.** List all the critical points in the interval.
**2.** Add the endpoints.
**3.** Plug every one into $f$. The **largest** value is the absolute max. The **smallest** value is the absolute min.

That's it. Try it.

slides.title: $f(x) = -x^2 + 3x - 2$ on $[1, 3]$
slides.hint: Set $-2x + 3 = 0$ and solve for $x$.
slides.afterCrit: Yes, only one critical point. Now add the two endpoints, $x = 1$ and $x = 3$.

slides.title: $f(x) = 3x^4 - 4x^3 - 12x^2 + 1$ on $[-2, 3]$
slides.hint: Set each factor of $12x(x - 2)(x + 1)$ equal to 0. All three answers are inside $[-2, 3]$.
slides.afterCrit: All three are inside the interval. Now add the endpoints.

slides.title: $f(x) = x^(3/5)(4 - x)$ on $[-1, 5]$
slides.hint: One critical point comes from the top being 0, and one from the bottom being 0.
slides.afterCrit: Both are inside the interval. Notice $x = 0$ is a critical point even though it will turn out not to be a max or min. It is only a suspect.

slides.title: Try it: $f(x) = x^3 - 12x - 5$ on $[-4, 6]$
slides.hint: Set $3x^2 - 12 = 0$. There are two solutions, and both are inside $[-4, 6]$.
slides.afterCrit: Both are inside the interval. Now add the endpoints.

slides.title: You have what you need
slides.text:
**Remember:**

• The absolute max and min are **heights** ($y$-values).
• The EVT: continuous on a closed interval means a max and min exist.
• Fermat: local max or min and differentiable means $f'(c) = 0$.
• $f'(c) = 0$ does **not** mean max or min.
• Critical points: $f' = 0$ or $f'$ does not exist. They are where to look.
• Absolute extremes on $[a, b]$: test the critical points and the endpoints.

Now try the drills.

questions.text: Global maximum and absolute maximum mean the same thing.
questions.explain: They are two names for the highest point on the graph.

questions.text: The absolute maximum of a function is an $x$-value.
questions.explain: The absolute maximum is a height, a $y$-value. The $x$-value is where it **occurs**.

questions.text: Which pair of conditions does the Extreme Value Theorem require?
options: $f$ is continuous on a closed interval
$f$ is differentiable on an open interval
$f'(x) = 0$ at some point of the interval
$f$ is increasing on the interval
questions.explain: The EVT needs a continuous function on a closed interval $[a, b]$.

questions.text: Which function is guaranteed by the EVT to have an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum?
options: $f(x) = tan x$ on $[0, pi]$
questions.explain: $x^3$ is continuous on the closed interval $[-2, 2]$. The first has an open interval, $1/x$ is undefined at 0, and $tan x$ is undefined at $pi/2$.

questions.text: The EVT applies to $f(x) = x^2$ on the open interval $(0, 3)$.
questions.explain: The interval is open, not closed, so the theorem does not apply.

questions.text: If the conditions of the EVT are not met, the function cannot have an absolute maximum.
questions.explain: The theorem only promises something when its conditions hold. Without them, a function may or may not have a maximum.

questions.text: A function that is continuous on $[a, b]$ must have both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on $[a, b]$.
questions.explain: That is exactly the Extreme Value Theorem.

questions.text: A local maximum is always the highest point on the whole graph.
questions.explain: A local maximum only has to be higher than the points near it.

questions.text: The absolute maximum of a continuous function on $[a, b]$ can occur at an endpoint.
questions.explain: The highest point can be at either end, as with $f(x) = x^2 + 1$ on $[-2, 2]$.

questions.text: A **critical point** of $f$ is an $x$-value where...
options: $f'(x) = 0$ or $f'(x)$ does not exist
$f'(x) = 0$ only
questions.explain: Critical points are where the derivative is 0 or does not exist.

questions.text: A critical point can occur where $f'(x)$ does not exist.
questions.explain: Sharp corners, cusps, and vertical tangents are critical points as long as $f$ is defined there.

questions.text: If $f'(c) = 0$, then $f$ has a local maximum or local minimum at $c$.
questions.explain: Fermat's Theorem does not work in reverse. $f(x) = x^3$ has $f'(0) = 0$ and no max or min.

questions.text: If $f$ has a local minimum at $c$ and $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then $f'(c) = 0$.
questions.explain: That is Fermat's Theorem.

questions.text: $f(x) = x^3$ has $f'(0) = 0$. What does this tell you?
options: $x = 0$ is a critical point, but you cannot tell yet if it is a max or min
$x = 0$ is a local maximum
$x = 0$ is a local minimum
$x = 0$ is not a critical point
questions.explain: A flat tangent makes it a critical point, but that is only a suspect. For $x^3$ the graph keeps climbing, so it is neither.

questions.text: $f(x) = |x|$ has a local minimum at $x = 0$, so Fermat's Theorem says $f'(0) = 0$.
questions.explain: $|x|$ is not differentiable at 0, so Fermat's Theorem does not apply. The point $x = 0$ is critical because $f'(0)$ does not exist.

questions.text: Critical points are the places where we should look for...
options: local maxima and minima
$x$-intercepts
vertical asymptotes
jumps in the graph
questions.explain: Local maxes and mins can only hide at critical points.

questions.text: To find the absolute maximum on $[a, b]$, you only need to check the critical points. The endpoints do not matter.
questions.explain: The highest point can be at an endpoint, so you must test the endpoints too.

questions.text: To find the absolute extremes of a continuous function on $[a, b]$: list the ___ points, add the ___, and plug them all into $f$. The ___ value is the max and the ___ value is the min.
questions.explain: Test every critical point and both endpoints. The largest value is the max and the smallest value is the min.

questions.text: $f(x) = cos x$ on all real numbers. Which is true?
options: Both an absolute max and an absolute min
An absolute max, but no absolute min
An absolute min, but no absolute max
Neither one
questions.explain: The graph rises to 1 and falls to $-1$ over and over. The absolute maximum is 1 and the absolute minimum is $-1$.

questions.text: $f(x) = x^3$ on all real numbers. Which is true?
options: Both an absolute max and an absolute min
An absolute max, but no absolute min
An absolute min, but no absolute max
Neither one
questions.explain: The graph climbs forever to the right and falls forever to the left.

questions.text: $f(x) = 1/(x^2 + 1)$ on all real numbers. Which is true?
options: Both an absolute max and an absolute min
An absolute max, but no absolute min
An absolute min, but no absolute max
Neither one
questions.explain: The highest point is $(0, 1)$. The graph only gets closer to 0 on the sides, so there is no lowest point.
The top of the hill is $(0, 1)$. The maximum is a height, so the answer is 1.
The graph peaks at height 1 many times. The absolute maximum is 1.
The graph bottoms out at height $-1$ many times. The absolute minimum is $-1$.
The highest point is $(4, 4)$. It occurs at $x = 4$.
The lowest point is $(2, 0)$. It occurs at $x = 2$.
The top of the hill is $(1, 3)$. The absolute maximum is 3.
The top of the hill is $(1, 3)$. It occurs at $x = 1$.
The left end $(-1, -1)$ is lower than the right end. The absolute minimum is $-1$.
The lowest point is the left end $(-1, -1)$. It occurs at $x = -1$.
The graph heads toward the open circle at $(0, 0)$ but never reaches it. There is no absolute minimum.
The graph heads toward the open circle at height 9 but never reaches it. There is no absolute maximum.
The highest point is the filled point $(0, 2)$. The absolute maximum is 2.
The highest point is $(0, 2)$. It occurs at $x = 0$.
The left piece heads down toward the open circle at height $-2$ but never reaches it, and the filled point is higher. There is no absolute minimum.
The lowest point is $(0, 0)$ where the graph starts.
The graph shoots upward near the dashed line, so there is no highest point.
The graph climbs forever to the right, so there is no absolute maximum.
The graph keeps climbing to the right. The hilltop is only a local maximum, so there is no absolute maximum.

questions.text:
Find the critical points of $f(x) = x^2 - 6x$.

Its derivative is $f'(x) = 2x - 6$.

Find the critical points of $f(x) = x^3 - 12x$.

Its derivative is $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12$.

Find the critical points of $f(x) = x^4 - 2x^2$.

Its derivative is $f'(x) = 4x^3 - 4x = 4x(x - 1)(x + 1)$.

Find the critical points of $f(x) = |x + 1|$.

Its derivative is $-1$ when $x < -1$ and $1$ when $x > -1$.
questions.explain: The derivative is never 0, but it does not exist at the corner $x = -1$.

questions.text:
Find the critical points of $f(x) = x^3 + 3x$.

Its derivative is $f'(x) = 3x^2 + 3$.
questions.explain: $3x^2 + 3 = 0$ has no solutions, and the derivative exists everywhere. There are no critical points.

questions.text:
Find the critical points of $f(x) = x^(2/3)$.

Its derivative is $f'(x) = 2 / (3x^(1/3))$.
questions.explain: The derivative is never 0, but it does not exist at $x = 0$ while $f(0)$ does. So $x = 0$ is a critical point.

questions.text:
Find the critical points of $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x$.

Its derivative is $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12x + 9$.

Find the critical points of $f(x) = x / (1 + x^2)$.

Its derivative is $f'(x) = (1 - x^2) / (1 + x^2)^2$.
questions.explain: The bottom is never 0. The top $1 - x^2$ is 0 at $x = -1$ and $x = 1$.

questions.text: Find the absolute **maximum** of $f(x) = 3x^2 - 9x$ on $[-1, 2]$.
questions.label: Absolute max =
questions.explain: $f'(x) = 6x - 9 = 0$ at $x = 1.5$. The critical point: $x = 1.5$. Test the endpoints too: $f(-1) = 12$; $f(1.5) = -6.75$; $f(2) = -6$. The largest is 12.

questions.text: Find the absolute **minimum** of $f(x) = 3x^2 - 9x$ on $[-1, 2]$.
questions.label: Absolute min =
